newsitem.title: SPAIN: Peru rebel leader warns of tragedy if force used.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebel leader warns of tragedy if force used.

text.p: The leader of Marxist rebels holding 72 people captive in the Japanese ambassador's home in Peru warned in an interview on Sunday that any use of force by Peruvian security forces would end in tragedy for the hostages.

Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolino said in an interview with Spanish newspapers El Pais and La Vanguardia he and his followers were ready to die if Peru resorts to military force to end the stand-off.
"We know (an assault by the Peruvian army) will be tragic for the gentlemen held captive here. We are sorry for them and for their families," Cerpa was quoted as saying.
"We are not afraid. If they decide to use force, they will find every one of us prepared for combat. We are aware that if things turn out this way, we will not leave alive."
The rebels seized the ambassador's residence on December 17 and took some 500 guests at a party hostage in a bid to free jailed comrades. All but 72 have since been freed.
Peruvian military manouevres recently around the ambassador's home have heightened fears of possible confrontation between security forces and the heavily-armed rebels inside.
Cerpa, 43, acknowledged one of his personal motives in the siege is to free his wife Nancy who is among the MRTA prisoners.
"I can't deny that it is one more motive because I love her and I am aware that our children need their mother," he said.
Cerpa said his wife, Nancy Gilvonio, was condemned to serve a life sentence in a maximum security prison.

"I think they have been cruel with Nancy because they imposed the punishment on her they could not impose on me," he said. "I want to emphasise that there are also other boys and girls of my comrades who need their mother and father...We did this for all of them."

Cerpa did not repeat the rebels' long-standing demand for liberation of the more than 400 MRTA prisoners as a condition for release of the hostages but said it must be among the key issues on the agenda in any talks with the government.

Cerpa noted this was a departure from the rebels' previous stance in which they demanded talks with the government focus solely on the release of prisoners, a condition rejected by the government. Cerpa said this disagreement had stalled negotiations between the government and the rebels.

The rebels will not free any more hostages, Cerpa said. Specifically, he rejected the release of Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela to participate in talks set for February 17 in Brazil on a border conflict with Ecuador.

Cerpa said his group has wanted and still wants a dialogue with the government about the nation's problems with the objective of achieving peace with social justice. He said the MRTA was prepared to lay down its arms if this goal could be achieved. "They never took us seriously," he said.
The Spanish newspapers said the interview with Cerpa was conducted on Friday via ham radio and Peruvian police monitoring the conversation interrupted periodically.
Reporters scanned radio frequencies for a week to find the one used by the rebels and establish contact, they said.
